articles.title: Employer health costs projected to rise 9.5 percent
articles.summary: A new risk analysis released by leading insurance broker Aon this week projected that employer health costs in the U.S. will rise by roughly 10 percent in 2027. Aon, the second largest global insurance broker, projected that at the current status quo, employer healthcare costs will rise by 9.5 percent next year. This would mean…
articles.body:
A new risk analysis released by leading insurance broker Aon this week projected that employer health costs in the U.S. will rise by roughly 10 percent in 2027.

Aon, the second largest global insurance broker, projected that at the current status quo, employer healthcare costs will rise by 9.5 percent next year. This would mean spending an added $19,000 per employee on average and would mark a fourth consecutive year of near-double-digit percentage increases.

The firm noted, however, that many employers will likely implement “cost-saving changes or programs” to mitigate expected costs.

Aon identified “rising medical utilization, chronic disease prevalence and growth in drug spending” as factors contributing to the rising costs.

Their projections found that health plan costs will rise across all industries, with the highest spikes anticipated for finance and insurance; technology and communication; and the public sector.

“Employers have now experienced several consecutive years of health care cost increases that are approaching double digits,” said Mike Pasterick, Aon’s North America health solutions leader, in a statement.

“At this level, rising health care costs become much more than a budgeting challenge and influence organizational decisions from benefits strategy and employee affordability to broader workforce and financial planning priorities,” he added. “Leaders are undergoing pressure to maintain affordable benefits while continuing to invest in attracting, supporting and retaining talent.”

articles.title: HHS launches autistic missing persons alert initiative
articles.summary: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced on Friday a new federal initiative to improve preparedness and response efforts when individuals with autism are reported missing. The agency will partner with the Department of Justice and the Federal Emergency Management Agency to strengthen coordination among emergency management agencies, law enforcement, first responders and…
articles.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced on Friday a new federal initiative to improve preparedness and response efforts when individuals with autism are reported missing.

The agency will partner with the Department of Justice and the Federal Emergency Management Agency to strengthen coordination among emergency management agencies, law enforcement, first responders and community partners nationwide.

Called the National Autism Missing and Endangered Person Alert Initiative, the program reflects a shared federal commitment to treat high-risk, autism-related missing person cases with appropriate urgency, according to HHS.

“When an autistic child or adult goes missing, every minute matters,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. “President Trump has made improving the lives of Americans with autism and their families a priority. We are bringing federal, state and local partners together to improve prevention, speed the response, and help bring autistic children and adults home safely.”

HHS said it will also establish a national framework of best practices for autism-related missing person cases, which will aim to address the leading causes of preventable injury and death among individuals with autism, like accidental drowning.

The initiative will build on existing missing and endangered person alert capabilities that help to get “critical information to authorities and the public quickly and helps bring missing persons home safely,” Kennedy said during a press conference.

“Alert faster, search smarter and save lives,” he added.

But Kennedy stressed HHS has only just started to design a framework; the system doesn’t exist yet.

“If an autistic loved one goes missing, people should call 911 immediately. And be ready to share critical information about communication, behavior, about the attraction of water,” Kennedy said.

Approximately half of children with autism engage in wandering behavior at some point, HHS said.

Drowning accounts for the majority of wandering fatalities, and many missing individuals are found close to their last known location.

The National Autism Safety Council reports that an average of eight children with autism die each month in the U.S. following wandering or elopement, most often from drowning in nearby water.

articles.title: Navy reportedly weighs naming aircraft carrier for Trump instead of Black Pearl Harbor hero
articles.summary: The name of Pearl Harbor hero Doris Miller could be removed from one of the U.S. Navy’s next aircraft carriers, with President Donald Trump’s name reportedly among those being considered as a replacement.
articles.body:
WACO, Texas ( KWKT ) — The name of Pearl Harbor hero Doris Miller could be removed from one of the U.S. Navy’s next aircraft carriers, with President Trump’s name reportedly among those being considered as a replacement.

The Navy has been discussing renaming the future USS Doris Miller, the Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier designated CVN-81, reports CNN . No decision has been formally announced.

The carrier was named for Miller in January 2020 during a ceremony at Pearl Harbor.

At the time, Acting Secretary of the Navy Thomas Modly said the selection recognized not only Miller, but generations of enlisted sailors.

“In selecting this name, we honor the contributions of all our enlisted ranks, past and present, men and women, of every race, religion and background,” Modly said.

The naming was historic. The USS Doris Miller would become the first U.S. aircraft carrier named for a Black American and the first named in honor of a sailor for actions performed while serving in the enlisted ranks.

Miller was born in Waco, Texas, on Oct. 12, 1919, and joined the Navy in 1939. He was serving aboard the battleship USS West Virginia when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941.

During the attack, Miller helped wounded sailors before manning an anti-aircraft gun and firing at Japanese planes, despite having no formal training on the weapon.

Miller was later awarded the Navy Cross for his actions, becoming the first Black American to receive the decoration.

Miller was killed in action in November 1943 when the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay was torpedoed and sunk during operations in the Pacific.

The Navy has also honored Miller before. The Knox-class frigate USS Miller entered service in 1973 and remained in commission until 1991.

Sources told CNN discussions of renaming the USS Doris Miller have been underway for months, with the ship increasingly referred to internally by its hull number, CVN-81.

The sources, which spoke to CNN anonymously, said Trump’s name is among those under consideration if the carrier is renamed.

Miller’s family told CNN they were not informed in advance about the possibility of his name being removed from the ship.

Official Navy historical records continue to identify CVN-81 as the future USS Doris Miller.

Nexstar’s KWKT reached out to the U.S. Navy’s Office of Information, who has said they do not have anything to share at this time.

articles.title: Reports of sexual assault in military dropped for third year in a row: Pentagon
articles.summary: Reports of sexual assault in the U.S. military dropped for the third year in a row in 2025, and the Pentagon received a slightly lower number of sexual harassment complaints last year compared with 2024, the department said in a report that was made public Friday. The Pentagon received a total of 7,998 reports of…
articles.body:
Reports of sexual assault in the U.S. military dropped for the third year in a row in 2025, and the Pentagon received a slightly lower number of sexual harassment complaints last year compared with 2024, the department said in a report that was made public Friday.

The Pentagon received a total of 7,998 reports of sexual assault in 2025, down from the previous year’s 8,195 reports. There were 8,515 reports of sexual assault in 2023 and 8,942 reports in 2022.

Out of the 7,998 reports in 2025, 5,022 were unrestricted reports and 2,976 remained restricted at the end of fiscal 2025, the Pentagon said in the 29-page report .

Unrestricted reports for sexual harassment or sexual assault are reported to the chain of command, and it results in an official probe, allowing service members to access mental healthcare and legal assistance.

“Dignity, respect and discipline are foundational to the warrior ethos and the overall preparedness of the force. Sexual assault and sexual harassment undermine these values, eroding trust and threatening the mission,” Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony J. Tata said in a statement .

“The FY 2025 report underscores our ongoing commitment to maintaining high standards, protecting our people, and building a unified, ready and lethal fighting force,” Tata said.

During 2025, the Pentagon received 2,936 sexual harassment complaints, a bit lower than in 2024 when the department got 3,014 complaints.

The Pentagon is obligated to send an annual report to Congress as outlined in Section 1631 of the 2011 Ike Skelton National Defense Authorization Act. The 2025 report was delivered to the Senate and House Armed Services committees, along with the House and Senate Veterans’ Affairs panels on Aug. 10.

The Marine Corps had the highest percentage of women experiencing unwanted sexual contact out of the service branches with 6.4 percent, followed by 5.1 percent in the Navy and 4.5 percent in the Army. The Air Force was the lowest at 2.8 percent.

Among men, the Navy was the highest at 1.5 percent in 2025. The Army and Marine Corps were at 1 percent, the report said.

The Pentagon said the estimated rate of unwanted sexual contact for active-duty women fell from 6.8 percent in 2023 to 4.3 percent in 2025. A third of victims came forward last year, an increase from a quarter in 2023.

“This statistically significant decrease in estimated prevalence was mostly driven by fewer enlisted women (E1-E4 and E5-E9) and junior officer women (O1-O3) as well as women ages 35 and younger indicating past-year unwanted sexual contact on the survey,” the department wrote in the report.

About 1 percent of active-duty men indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact in 2025, a slight decrease from 2023 when it was at 1.3 percent.

Around 20,492 active service members — 9,860 active-duty women and 10,632 active-duty men — experienced unwanted sexual contact last year, a drop from 2023 when 29,061 active duty said the same.

Outside groups pointed to the 2025 figure being nearly 40 percent higher than in 2016, when it was 14,900, and last year’s numbers being roughly identical to 2018, with 20,500.

About a third of service members who indicated experiencing unwanted sexual contact last year reported the incident to their authority, an increase from a quarter in 2023.

The Pentagon had “sufficient” evidence to take disciplinary action in 1,321 cases of individuals probed for an allegation of sexual assault, the department said in the report.

Josh Connolly, the senior vice president of Protect Our Defenders, a nonprofit group that works to end sexual misconduct in the military, said he would not take the Pentagon’s figures at “face value” and neither should the public.

“Survivors are more afraid to come forward than they were two years ago, and this administration has spent the past year giving them reason to be – rolling back whistleblower protections, making it harder to report anonymously, warning people who come forward that they may be punished for it,” Connolly said in a statement Friday. “A number that falls because people stopped talking is not progress.”

Early last year, the Navy halted sexual assault prevention and response training. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in October last year that he would revamp offices with the Pentagon’s inspector general office and the department’s equal employment opportunity office that allowed service members to anonymously file whistleblower complaints.

“Talk to those who do report,” Connolly said Friday. “The vast majority of those cases go nowhere. Documents get lost. Evidence never gets used. They’re handed from one lawyer to the next, or never get one at all. Then they’re pushed out and lose their medical and mental health care on the way.”

articles.title: TikTok reaches $400M settlement with DOJ over alleged children’s privacy law violations
articles.summary: TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, have agreed to pay $400 million to settle with the Department of Justice (DOJ) over allegations the platform violated a children’s online privacy law, the agency said Friday. The company will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million after a court dismisses an earlier consent decree entered against…
articles.body:
TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, have agreed to pay $400 million to settle with the Department of Justice (DOJ) over allegations the platform violated a children’s online privacy law, the agency said Friday.

The company will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million after a court dismisses an earlier consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, known as Musical.ly, according to the DOJ.

The DOJ sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024, accusing the video-based social media app of violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). The law bars online platforms from collecting data on users younger than 13 years without their parents’ consent.

The government alleged that the company allowed kids younger than 13 to create accounts and failed to delete their accounts and information when asked by parents.

“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said in a statement.

“The Department’s priority is ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations,” he continued. “This resolution secures a substantial recovery while reinforcing the protections that families expect and deserve.”

The Hill has reached out to TikTok for comment.

The DOJ noted in a press release that TikTok has “undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices” since it brought the lawsuit two years ago.

The platform is now under the control of TikTok USDS Joint Venture, an entity that is majority owned by American investors, after Congress passed a law in 2024 requiring ByteDance to divest from the app or face a U.S. ban.

The push for the divest-or-ban law stemmed from national security and privacy concerns about ByteDance’s ties to China. President Trump repeatedly pushed back the deadline to enforce the ban after taking office, as he sought to strike a deal with Beijing to keep the app available in the U.S.

Trump signed off on a deal to turn over TikTok to the joint venture last September. ByteDance maintained a 19.9 percent stake in the company, while Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX each received a 15 percent stake and are considered managing investors.

articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Friday that alfalfa sprouts are linked to a current E. coli and salmonella outbreak. The agency has tied several foodborne illness cases to the consumption of alfalfa sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands, also urging Americans who have purchased the affected sprouts to throw…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Friday that alfalfa sprouts are linked to a current E. coli and salmonella outbreak.

The agency has tied several foodborne illness cases to the consumption of alfalfa sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands, also urging Americans who have purchased the affected sprouts to throw them away or return them.

The contaminated alfalfa sprouts have sparked the third ongoing salmonella outbreak this month and second E. coli ongoing outbreak since the beginning of the year. In late July, the agency identified certain shelled eggs as a source of salmonella and later recalled some frozen blueberries for posing a severe risk of E. coli infection.

As of Friday, the CDC announced that the 55 reported cases were spread across 15 states, with four cases resulting in hospitalization. While interviewing the infected people, 76 percent had reported eating the sprouts in the week before they got sick.

Most people impacted by the outbreak only contracted one of the illnesses — with 46 contracting E. coli and seven salmonella. The remaining two caught both.

But the CDC estimates the number could be higher, as it’s common for those infected with salmonella and E. coli to recover without receiving medical care.

The CDC said it believes the outbreak began between May 31 and Aug. 8, and traceback data tied infections to alfalfa from Calco and Everything Sprouts — both sold at grocery stores and used in restaurants.

Cases in Minnesota and Wisconsin accounted for nearly 70 percent of recorded infections. The CDC traced back some of these cases to restaurants in both states that reported using Everything Sprouts-branded alfalfa.

Officials are continuing to investigate the outbreak, which involves three different strains of E. coli and one strain of salmonella.

Salmonella is a common foodborne illness causing diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps. The CDC estimates that these symptoms can emerge between six hours and six days after infection and last four to seven days.

Common symptoms of an E. coli infection are similar to salmonella but can also include stomach cramps, bloody stool or urine, vomiting and dehydration, according to the Food and Drug Administration . They can begin just a few days to as many as nine days after ingesting E. coli bacteria.

Investigators found the percentage of infected people who ate alfalfa was much higher than the number of Americans who report eating it, supporting their finding that the sprout caused the illness.

The CDC’s FoodNet Population survey — used to estimate how often Americans eat foods commonly linked to illness — found only 8.7 percent of respondents had eaten the sprouts within the past seven days.

articles.title: Interior shuffles several senior career staffers
articles.summary: The Interior Department has recently shuffled at least 25 senior career staffers, giving them different roles at the department that oversees the nation’s public lands, parks and other resources, a source familiar told The Hill. The employees who were shuffled to new positions at the department belong to the senior executive service (SES), a group…
articles.body:
The Interior Department has recently shuffled at least 25 senior career staffers, giving them different roles at the department that oversees the nation’s public lands, parks and other resources, a source familiar told The Hill.

The employees who were shuffled to new positions at the department belong to the senior executive service (SES), a group of highly experienced upper-level officials who are career staffers rather than political appointees.

The specific reasons for the shuffle are not entirely clear. Reached for comment, an Interior Department spokesperson said that while it does not comment on individual personnel matters, “SES reassignments are a routine management tool used across administrations.”

“The Department continues to align senior leadership and resources to best support its mission, improve organizational effectiveness and deliver results for the American people,” said the spokesperson, who did not sign their name to the email.

The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to make changes to the federal workforce — and in particular has sought to downsize it.

Last fall, Interior considered cutting hundreds of jobs , though the widespread cuts it floated at the time did not appear to come to fruition.

articles.title: Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor in chief, publisher, reporter
articles.summary: The Pentagon fired the publisher, editor in chief and at least one reporter at Stars and Stripes, a historically independent military news outlet, Friday as the department has looked to reshape its coverage in recent months. The Department of Defense (DOD) dismissed Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin, publisher Max Lederer and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte, Stars…
articles.body:
The Pentagon fired the publisher, editor in chief and at least one reporter at Stars and Stripes, a historically independent military news outlet, Friday as the department has looked to reshape its coverage in recent months.

The Department of Defense (DOD) dismissed Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin, publisher Max Lederer and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte, Stars and Stripes reported Friday .

Slavin said he was ousted for insubordination after telling CBS News in an interview that potential censorship of news for U.S. service members would be a red line.

Korte confirmed her firing on social media, saying it was for “insubordination after I told a CBS reporter that I work for Stars and Stripes – not the Pentagon, not any administration, and not any policy maker.”

“I consider it a great privilege to live alongside members of the military and share their stories. It’s a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution and deserve the right to a free and independent press,” Korte said on social platform X .

Stars and Stripes has traditionally enjoyed independence from the DOD, even though its staff are Pentagon employees and it’s partially funded by the department.

Earlier this week, Lederer said he would retire from his role by Sept. 30, since his “understanding of the value and mission” of the outlet is different in “fundamental ways” from the plans the DOD has for the newspaper.

“I have thought a great deal about the right time to step aside, and I have concluded that this is it,” Lederer said in a note to staff. “I leave with real pride in what we have accomplished together and with complete confidence in what you will accomplish next.”

The DOD installed Navy Capt. William Urban, an active duty service member, as the new deputy publisher a few weeks ago, prompting questions from three Democratic senators.

Journalism groups slammed the Pentagon for ousting Slavin, arguing it is another attempt by the department to dictate news coverage of the outlet.

“This is an assault on the fundamental principle that journalists must be free to report the news without fear of retaliation from the government officials they cover,” the National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in a statement Friday . “The Pentagon must reaffirm that principle and make clear that Stars and Stripes journalists will not be punished for doing their jobs.”

The Pentagon has sought to refocus coverage on “warfighting” and remove what it calls “woke distractions” in the outlet’s coverage.

“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Pentagon Chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January.

In April, the DOD removed the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, the person in charge of monitoring the outlet’s editorial independence and reporting concerns to Congress.

“Apparently the Pentagon also doesn’t want you to hear from me anymore about threats to the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes,” Smith wrote in an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal at the time.

articles.title: Teen drops high-profile social media addiction lawsuit
articles.summary: A teenager has dropped her lawsuit against Meta, YouTube and Snapchat, which was set to go to trial later this year as part of a broader series of cases accusing social media giants of designing addictive platforms. The teen, referred to as P.M.Y., previously settled with TikTok and “chose to dismiss the remainder so she…
articles.body:
A teenager has dropped her lawsuit against Meta, YouTube and Snapchat, which was set to go to trial later this year as part of a broader series of cases accusing social media giants of designing addictive platforms.

The teen, referred to as P.M.Y., previously settled with TikTok and “chose to dismiss the remainder so she could try to resume her life,” her attorney Emily Jeffcott said in a statement.

“PMY initiated this process with the goal of holding social media companies accountable and to push for changes to protect young people like herself,” Jeffcott said, adding, “She is ready to close this chapter and focus on moving forward.”

She had accused the companies of contributing to her social media addiction, depression and self-harm, according to Reuters.

Thousands of lawsuits against the companies have been consolidated into a single legal proceeding in Los Angeles Superior Court. Her lawsuit was scheduled to be heard by a jury in October as a bellwether trial, which are used as test cases for the broader litigation.

The first trial got underway in January. A jury ultimately found Meta and YouTube liable for negligently designing their platforms in March and ordered the companies to pay a combined $6 million. Both Snapchat and TikTok settled the case before trial.

R.K.C., the minor bringing another case set to go to trial, ultimately settled with Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube, and dropped his lawsuit against Meta last month.

“Another plaintiff in the personal injury trials has dropped her case against Meta after settling with TikTok,” Meta said in a statement after P.M.Y. opted to dismiss her lawsuit.

“This plaintiff had a significant mental health condition that pre-dated her use of social media, and it’s clear that many of these cases fit the same pattern,” the company added. “We’ll continue defending ourselves vigorously in court.”

Google spokesperson José Castaneda noted in a statement that P.M.Y. “voluntarily withdrew their claims against YouTube without payment.” Google is YouTube’s parent company.

He suggested this affirms the company’s “longstanding position that we provide safe, age-appropriate experiences and strong parental controls for young people and families.”

A spokesperson for Snap Inc., the owner of Snapchat, said in a statement that the company remains “focused on strengthening the safeguards, tools, and educational resources that support the safety, privacy, and well-being of all Snapchatters.”

articles.summary: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is looking to leave his role at the Pentagon around the end of 2026 following a months-long turf war with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former White House official and another source familiar with the discussions told The Hill on Friday. A third source familiar said Driscoll has long communicated that…
articles.body:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is looking to leave his role at the Pentagon around the end of 2026 following a months-long turf war with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former White House official and another source familiar with the discussions told The Hill on Friday.

A third source familiar said Driscoll has long communicated that between 23 and 24 months is the lifetime of an Army secretary in the Trump administration. Driscoll, an ally of Vice President Vance, was confirmed by the Senate on Feb. 25 last year in a 66-28 vote.

Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment.

A U.S. official, granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, told The Hill on Saturday they have heard a similar timeline for Driscoll’s departure.

The Army Secretary has pushed the service branch to improve living conditions for service members, modernize equipment and learn from Ukrainian forces how to utilize commercial technology in modern warfare.

One of the sources familiar said Driscoll has been “aggressive” in getting buy-in from general officers to spearhead and deliver on these efforts, given his limited tenure.

During his tenure, Driscoll, a former venture capitalist, formed a close working relationship with the former Army’s chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, who was ousted from his role in early April by Hegseth.

President Trump and Hegseth then picked Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff , to serve as the Army’s acting chief of staff. LaNeve, who is a former military aide to Hegseth, has met with senators in recent months, but his confirmation is in question over objections from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

The Army Secretary has also been involved in a simmering battle for influence with Hegseth, with tension flaring late last year when Trump picked Driscoll to negotiate with Ukrainian officials in hopes of ending the Russia-Ukraine war, The Hill previously reported .

Last year, Driscoll and George, whose firing has drawn criticism from GOP lawmakers , rolled out the so-called Army Transformation Initiative last year, which was intended to focus on three areas: “deliver critical warfighting capabilities, optimize our force structure and eliminate waste and obsolete programs.”

Among the fields of focus were integrating drones and artificial intelligence into Army formations,

Driscoll’s expected departure was reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal.

The Army is planning to phase out a unit that was studying and incorporating lessons from overseas wars, including the use of unmanned systems in the Russia-Ukraine war, The Hill reported on Thursday.

The battalion, part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade, was backed by senior Army leadership, including George and Gen. Chris Donahue, the former commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa.

This story was updated at 4:09 p.m. on Aug. 22, 2026.

articles.title: 5 things to know about the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington
articles.summary: The streets of Washington will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever during the final stretch of its 2026 season. The event, which spans two days and will close streets around the National Mall…
articles.body:
The streets of Washington will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever during the final stretch of its 2026 season.

The event, which spans two days and will close streets around the National Mall and downtown D.C., is being billed as one of the final spectacles commemorating the country’s 250th birthday at the behest of President Trump.

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of Sunday’s Grand Prix in D.C.

Sunday’s race will mark a dramatic conclusion to a summer in D.C. that came with a slew of major sports and cultural events presided over by Trump’s administration.

The president hosted the Great American State Fair, facilitated a UFC primetime fight just outside the White House and delivered an address to the nation on July 4 before one of the largest fireworks displays downtown D.C. has seen.

This weekend’s race was not on the initial 2026 IndyCar schedule, and it came at Trump’s behest.

Trump reportedly had been musing about a road race on D.C. streets for months, and in January, he directed the departments of Transportation and the Interior to designate a race route through the National Mall.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix will serve as the first auto race held on the streets of the nation’s capital, with organizers saying this week it will likely be a “one-and-done” event.

Top Trump administration officials, like Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, are seeking to cast the event as a moment of unity for the country.

“And I think if you look at the political divide in America, this is an event that brings America together,” Duffy told the New York Post this week. “Cars and racing is freedom and American.”

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are expected to take a ceremonial lap around the course in “The Beast” on Sunday before the race starts, likely drawing even more attention to the unique end-of-summer showcase.

IndyCar looking to create the right ‘visuals’

The race for the IndyCar championship is entering its final stretch, and several of the sport’s top names will be racing this weekend in D.C.

Series points leader Álex Palou will be in the field, along with top-ranked American Kyle Kirkwood, both of whom feature cars built by Honda Racing.

The action starts Saturday with two practice races. Qualifying is set for that afternoon.

Sunday’s race day activities will begin with a warmup at 9 a.m. before President Trump waves the green flag at 1 p.m.

Those who follow the sport closely say Sunday’s spectacle will be a major moment for a racing league that has catered largely to a niche audience for decades.

“It’s all about the visual for me. You know, time and place,” longtime motor sports journalist Curt Cavin wrote this week. “The visuals of the U.S. Capitol, Washington Monument, White House and the rest of the elements that make the city the most recognizable in the world will give the sport much-craved relevance. Everything else is secondary, including the actual race, which at close to three hours will be interesting in itself. Let’s see how cool all of this looks.”

Race day will have a major impact on life in D.C.

The buildout for Sunday’s race has been underway for weeks, closing city streets and making things difficult for commuters during a usually sleepy time of year in the district, when schools are closed and Congress is on recess.

In addition to the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns or 147 laps, IndyCar has put up massive hospitality suites, fenced off sidewalks on major downtown thoroughfares and left much of the usually busy National Mall unpassable to vehicle or pedestrian traffic during the tourist season.

Local officials have been urging D.C. residents who do not plan to attend the race to stay away from the area all weekend, while those who do have tickets should seek public transportation to get to their designated viewing areas.

“This is worse than cherry blossom,” D.C. commuter Nancy Marlow told local radio station WTOP this week, referencing the annual springtime festival that draws thousands to D.C.’s Tidal Basin. “I’ve been out here over an hour. This time of year, it normally takes me 20 minutes.”

Other spots further from the racetrack have also been impacted, like the small streets near the Lincoln Memorial, which was closed briefly Friday while a promo for the race’s television coverage was being filmed.

Anyone who has ever been to an IndyCar race knows the races are, if nothing else, loud and can cause the ground to shake.

This has been a major point of concern for D.C. residents, business owners and operators of iconic district museums and art galleries that are either directly along the racetrack or not far away.

In a letter sent to the National Park Service late last month, the nonprofit New Living Deal raised concern the race “may harm historic properties directly adjacent to the race course.”

“Such vibrations are well above normal street traffic and even go beyond those of jackhammers, pile drivers, and even freight trains, which are commonly mitigated pieces of equipment during construction projects for noise as well as vibration due to their extremely high potential for impacts,” the nonprofit wrote. “Like many others across the nation, we question the necessity and cost of this event and seek clarity about the steps we assume are already being taken to mitigate adverse effects and harm to historic structures surrounding the proposed race course.”

A spokesperson for the National Gallery of Art told WTOP it had conducted a vibration study in preparation for the race and put forth “a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities.”

Spanning 1.7 miles, Sunday’s race will wind through some of D.C.’s most notable downtown streets and pass dozens of iconic landmarks and federal buildings.

The start and finish line has been placed on 3rd Street NW between Pennsylvania and Maryland avenues, just blocks from the U.S. Capitol.

Racers’ first turn will be west on Pennsylvania Avenue, where they will speed past the National Gallery of Art and National Archives before heading south on 9th Street NW past the Smithsonian.

The race track turns again on 7th Street NW through the heart of the National Mall, where the White House and Capitol will be most visible from inside a racer’s vehicle.

The final stretch of the race will come along Independence Avenue SW, where drivers will head east before a sharp left turn at the National Museum of the American Indian and up 3rd Street NW toward the finish line and Delta 250 suites full of VIPs set to include President Trump.

Those who follow the sport closely say Sunday’s spectacle will be a major moment for a racing league that has catered largely to a niche audience for decades.

“It’s all about the visual for me. You know, time and place,” longtime motor sports journalist Curt Cavin wrote this week. “The visuals of the U.S. Capitol, Washington Monument, White House and the rest of the elements that make the city the most recognizable in the world will give the sport much-craved relevance. Everything else is secondary, including the actual race, which at close to three hours will be interesting in itself. Let’s see how cool all of this looks.”
Race day will have a major impact on life in D.C.

The buildout for Sunday’s race has been underway for weeks, closing city streets and making things difficult for commuters during a usually sleepy time of year in the district, when schools are closed and Congress is on recess.

In addition to the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns or 147 laps, IndyCar has put up massive hospitality suites, fenced off sidewalks on major downtown thoroughfares and left much of the usually busy National Mall unpassable to vehicle or pedestrian traffic during the tourist season.

Local officials have been urging D.C. residents who do not plan to attend the race to stay away from the area all weekend, while those who do have tickets should seek public transportation to get to their designated viewing areas.

“This is worse than cherry blossom,” D.C. commuter Nancy Marlow told local radio station WTOP this week, referencing the annual springtime festival that draws thousands to D.C.’s Tidal Basin. “I’ve been out here over an hour. This time of year, it normally takes me 20 minutes.”

Other spots further from the racetrack have also been impacted, like the small streets near the Lincoln Memorial, which was closed briefly Friday while a promo for the race’s television coverage was being filmed.
Anyone who has ever been to an IndyCar race knows the races are, if nothing else, loud and can cause the ground to shake.
This has been a major point of concern for D.C. residents, business owners and operators of iconic district museums and art galleries that are either directly along the racetrack or not far away.
In a letter sent to the National Park Service late last month, the nonprofit New Living Deal raised concern the race “may harm historic properties directly adjacent to the race course.”

“Such vibrations are well above normal street traffic and even go beyond those of jackhammers, pile drivers, and even freight trains, which are commonly mitigated pieces of equipment during construction projects for noise as well as vibration due to their extremely high potential for impacts,” the nonprofit wrote. “Like many others across the nation, we question the necessity and cost of this event and seek clarity about the steps we assume are already being taken to mitigate adverse effects and harm to historic structures surrounding the proposed race course.”

A spokesperson for the National Gallery of Art told WTOP it had conducted a vibration study in preparation for the race and put forth “a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities.”
Spanning 1.7 miles, Sunday’s race will wind through some of D.C.’s most notable downtown streets and pass dozens of iconic landmarks and federal buildings.
The start and finish line has been placed on 3rd Street NW between Pennsylvania and Maryland avenues, just blocks from the U.S. Capitol.
Racers’ first turn will be west on Pennsylvania Avenue, where they will speed past the National Gallery of Art and National Archives before heading south on 9th Street NW past the Smithsonian.
The race track turns again on 7th Street NW through the heart of the National Mall, where the White House and Capitol will be most visible from inside a racer’s vehicle.

The final stretch of the race will come along Independence Avenue SW, where drivers will head east before a sharp left turn at the National Museum of the American Indian and up 3rd Street NW toward the finish line and Delta 250 suites full of VIPs set to include President Trump.

articles.title: Cases of ‘scromiting’ condition tied to cannabis use spike among teens, young adults: New study
articles.summary: The syndrome has long been linked to chronic use of marijuana.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — The condition known to cause “scromiting” among some marijuana users has become more prevalent in the U.S., a recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows, though the trend among a specific age group may contradict previous understandings of the syndrome.

Cannabis (or cannabinoid) hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is as serious as it sounds. The condition, which can cause excessive vomiting with recurring bouts of severe stomach pain and nausea, was first detected in Australia two decades ago. Some have referred to a combination of CHS symptoms – screaming, due to the intense pain , and vomiting – as “scromiting.”

Hot showers and baths are often described as the only way to mitigate the discomfort. In rare cases, the condition has resulted in death, health officials said.

“[Patients] are not high in any fashion and in fact are in significant distress with uncontrolled vomiting, gagging, hurling, and pain,” Dr. Sam Torbati, the medical director of the Ruth and Harry Roman Emergency Department at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, explained to Nexstar via email. He sees patients already diagnosed with or presenting with suspected cases of cannabis hyperemesis arrive in his emergency department weekly.

It’s not limited to his emergency department either.

Virginia authorities reported that emergency department visits for CHS have jumped almost 29% since 2020. Significant spikes have also been reported in Massachusetts , Northern California , and parts of North Carolina. An official at Duke Regional Hospital in Durham, North Carolina, said last summer that patients with CHS are seen “every week, if not every day.”

In October, the World Health Organization added CHS to its diagnostic manual, a move meant to make it easier for health care providers to report the specific diagnosis rather than an overview of a patient’s symptoms. Patients may have otherwise been misdiagnosed as having another condition, like cyclic vomiting syndrome, according to a 2025 study .

A new report from the CDC found that, as expected , emergency department visits involving CHS increased in the months after the WHO’s update. While researchers noted the rise “[suggests] improved recognition” of CHS, it could indicate that “the public health impact” of the condition was previously underestimated.

The report also showed a concerning trend.

Health experts have frequently described CHS as occurring in long-time, chronic cannabis users. A George Washington University study of more than 1,000 people who reported experiencing CHS found that over 40% said they used marijuana more than five times a day. Roughly the same proportion of people said they had regularly used marijuana for more than five years before experiencing CHS.

However, the CDC’s latest report found “higher proportions” of emergency department visits involving CHS among younger persons.

From January 2023 to September 2025, patients between the ages of 15 and 24 had the highest average proportion of monthly emergency department visits at nearly 10 per 10,000. After the diagnostic code for CHS was introduced back in October, the CDC found that the rate jumped to nearly 39 per 10,000. The next–highest age group, 25- to 34-year-olds, had a rate of 28 per 10,000.

For comparison, the national average rate was 3.19 per 10,000 between 2023 and 2025. It jumped to nearly 12 per 10,000 in the eight months after the WHO’s update, the CDC determined.

The increase in younger people diagnosed with the syndrome “was actually one of the surprising findings for us,” CDC’s Alana Vivolo-Kantor, the study’s first author, told The Associated Press.

“Because the assumption going in was, ‘well, how can they have chronic use?’” she said. “How early were they using cannabis?”

Researchers noted the trend, explaining that “emerging evidence indicates that symptom onset can occur much sooner than was previously estimated, including within the first year of cannabis use.”

The report theorized that, among younger people, there may be changes in cannabis use behavior, like starting at an earlier age and using “evolving methods of use” like vaping or higher-potency products.

“Older data suggested CHS to occur after prolonged use but we are now seeing patients with CHS after only a few years of heavy cannabinoid use. This may be due to the higher potency of [marijuana] products which have much higher THC concentrations than in the past,” he said.

Recent studies had warned that younger people could be more at risk of experiencing CHS.

A study out of Massachusetts found that younger adults, ages 18 to 34, could be at a higher risk of experiencing CHS, as could Hispanic and Black individuals. A similar 2025 study of nationwide data found CHS was most common among those ages 16 to 34 and corresponded with heavier cannabis use. The same study found CHS was “notably more prevalent in the South,” but that those who reported the highest rates of cannabis use were in states that have legalized recreational cannabis, which are primarily in other regions.

Still, Torbati said that the condition impacts only a small proportion of people who use cannabis products. It’s also possible that a chronic user never develops CHS, health experts say .

It’s not clear exactly how marijuana products cause CHS, though Cedars Sinai said it may be brought on by receptors in the brain no longer responding to marijuana as they had before.

CHS can occur in three phases: prodromal, hyperemetic, and recovery.

During the first, which “may last for months or years,” patients can experience belly pain and nausea in the morning. This may lead to increased marijuana use, as it is often used to treat such symptoms.

In the hyperemetic phase, symptoms can become worse and progress to vomiting that is “overwhelming” and “recurrent,” lasting about a day or two. Patients may feel the need to bathe frequently, as hot water has been known to ease their nausea. It’s during this phase that health experts say patients typically seek medical care.

During the final phase, recovery, symptoms fade over time before disappearing as the patient stops using any and all forms of cannabis. Symptoms are known to return if they try marijuana again, however.

“[The] majority of patients have been diagnosed with CHS in the past and are either in denial or unable to stop use of marijuana products,” he explained. “These patients often will not provide accurate drug use histories, making the clinician’s job more challenging, often leading to unnecessary testing such as imaging with CT or ultrasound to rule out other conditions.”

They may further require “help from drug treatment specialists.”

While there are treatment options to control the symptoms patients can experience, the “long term cure to this condition requires abstinence from cannabinoid products,” Torbati said.

The CDC report, meanwhile, argued that there is a need to raise awareness of the condition among healthcare providers and the public, “but further education efforts might be needed to prevent the cause of CHS: cannabis use.”

Researchers also called for continued surveillance of the condition, “including the potential role of high-potency THC and hemp-derived products.”

If you believe you’re experiencing symptoms of CHS, health experts recommend speaking with your doctor.

articles.title: FTC moves to make retailers disclose use of ‘personalized pricing’ as technology now enables broad consumer surveillance
articles.summary: The proposal would warn companies that failing to disclose that they are using personal data to set prices could violate the FTC Act’s prohibition on unfair...
articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission is moving to ensure companies disclose use of customers' personal data to set prices, as technology makes it easier for retailers to tailor them to individual shoppers.

The FTC said that it is seeking public comment on an enforcement policy statement concerning "personalized pricing," which the agency defines as using personal data to determine how much a company believes an individual consumer is willing to spend. The proposal would warn companies that failing to disclose that they are using personal data to set prices could violate the FTC Act's prohibition on unfair or deceptive practices.

"When consumers see a listed price, they expect it to be the same price that everyone else sees, not the retailer's estimate of how much they are willing to pay based on their personal data," FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a press release. "The FTC does not have the legal authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances, but businesses that fail to tell consumers how their personal data is being used to set a price may be in violation of the FTC Act and other laws we enforce."

The FTC did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune . The proposal is open for public comment through Sept. 18.

The regulator's action comes after more than two years of scrutiny into what it calls "surveillance pricing." In July 2024, the FTC ordered eight companies involved in pricing technology to provide information about how they use customer data—including location, demographics, credit history and browsing or shopping history to help companies determine prices.

"Americans deserve to know whether businesses are using detailed consumer data to deploy surveillance pricing," then FTC Chair Lina M. Khan said at the time, "and the FTC's inquiry will shed light on this shadowy ecosystem of pricing middlemen."

The FTC's January 2025 findings said pricing intermediaries could use information ranging from a consumer's precise location and browser history to shopping behavior and even mouse movements to help retailers tailor prices or promotions. The agency said the companies it examined had worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery retailers.

The deep dive into personalized pricing comes after the FTC recently flagged dynamic pricing—or setting prices based on supply and demand as well as inventory levels and competitor pricing.

An FTC research document noted that companies using e-commerce websites or electronic shelf labels could potentially make price changes with similar frequency.

articles.title: US Treasury to stick to debt auction schedule despite bigger buybacks, Bessent says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The U. Treasury will continue with its regularly scheduled debt auctions, including for long-dated bonds, despite its move to...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The U.S. Treasury will continue with its regularly scheduled debt auctions, including for long-dated bonds, despite its move to increase buyback sizes of 10- to 30-year securities, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday.

Asked at a news ‌conference focused on Iran sanctions about Treasury's plans for bond buybacks and auction sizes going forward, Bessent said the department would "continue with our regular ‌program of auctions" announced in early August.

He added that the Treasury hasn't purchased any bonds yet in the enlarged buybacks, which will start on September 10 for 10- and 20-year securities.

Bessent, a former hedge ​fund manager with extensive experience in sovereign debt and currency markets, last week surprised global bond investors by announcing the Treasury would double the size of its quarterly repurchases of longer-dated bonds after their yields reached the highest levels in nearly two decades.

The Treasury chief's tactic helped bring down yields on 10-year Treasury notes and 20- and 30-year bonds for a short time, providing the administration some relief from the high bond yields that are rapidly driving up federal debt service costs. But yields on the longer-dated ‌maturities had largely retraced those drops by the end of ⁠the week. They were down modestly on Monday.

Bessent also warned countries on Monday to cut business ties to Iran, threatening them with secondary sanctions if they failed to do so, while stopping short of imposing severe penalties. He warned that a major sanctions ⁠announcement related to a bank would happen later this week.

He has not indicated the funding source for the Treasury buybacks, but the Treasury General Account at the Federal Reserve provides one source. Tapping that account would spare the need to finance the buybacks by issuing new, shorter-dated Treasuries, but would eat into the nation's cash reserves.

Unlike the Fed, the Treasury does ​not ​have the ability to create money at will, so it needs to pay for the ​buybacks from existing cash resources or borrow the funds. Any additional ‌borrowing would need to be done at shorter maturities so as not to upend the goal of the buybacks, which is to boost liquidity in the market for longer-dated bonds.

The TGA is essentially the federal government's checking account, used to pay for daily government operations like federal worker salaries, defense contracts and Treasury interest and principal obligations. It stood at about $940 billion as of last Wednesday.

articles.title: This is how much one study says tariffs will cost US households
articles.summary: The Yale Budget Lab's estimate included newly announced tariffs on Canada.
articles.body:
United States tariffs will cost the typical American household more than $1,000 per year, the non-partisan Yale Budget Lab found in an estimate released on Tuesday.

The forecast arrives amid a flurry of fresh levies imposed on Canadian products after a collapse in trade negotiations over the weekend.

A round of 50% U.S. tariffs on dozens of Canadian goods worth $20 billion took effect on Saturday, followed by a measure unveiled on Monday that will double levies on Canadian cars and auto parts in January.

The US-Canada trade war could push up these prices, analysts say

The new tariffs on Canadian goods accounted for about $30 extra per household per year, the Yale Budget Lab said.

Canada on Tuesday announced levies of its own, to take effect on Sept. 8, that would match the value of goods targeted by U.S. tariffs.

Trump sharply criticized Canada for trade policies that he considers unfair toward U.S. products.

"On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with," Trump said on his social media platform on Monday. "They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!"

The rebuke arrived after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issued blistering remarks about the U.S. approach to trade negotiations. He said talks broke down after American negotiators made requests that were unfavorable to Canada.

"They asked too much and offered too little," Carney said at a Saturday press conference.

It all comes weeks after Trump slapped sweeping new tariffs on 60 trade partners, including the European Union. Those levies ramped up an effort to reconstruct far-reaching duties struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

Importers typically offset the tax burden of tariffs in the form of higher prices for shoppers. The new levies, as a result, threaten to strain household budgets at a time when the Iran war is already pushing up prices.

Inflation eased slightly in July, the most recent month on record, but price increases stayed above the pace recorded before a surge in fuel prices set off by the Middle East conflict.

Trump floats renaming Lake Ontario to 'Lake America,' denies claim he'd interfere with Canadians speaking French

Prices rose 3.4% in July compared to a year earlier, putting them more than a percentage point higher than the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2%.

The Iran war drove up gasoline prices and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May. A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief, but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting over ensuing weeks caused crude prices to climb.

The national average price of a gallon of gas registered at $4.09 on Tuesday, AAA data showed, marking a 37% rise since the outbreak of war in late February.

ABC News' Elizabeth Schulze contributed to this report.
